deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text. It is a constructed figure that belongs to the geometric 'criterion for biquadratic residues', whose main steps Gauss writes out on the next page (11). The bracket function on the previous page (10) is the counting tool for it.

(a) Lattice. Crosses and dots alternate in every row, and alternate rows are offset. Taking the dot/cross spacing as the unit (about 41 px both ways), the marks together form the Gaussian integers Z[i]. The two kinds of mark form a checkerboard: they are the two residue classes mod (1+i), i.e. the parity of x+y.

(b) 'Full quadrant' of M. The large tilted square has two corners circled at lattice points. My reading (mine, from measurement) is to put 0 at the lower-left circled point. Then the edges are M ≈ 19+4i (to the lower right, about 780 px right and 160 px up) and iM ≈ -4+19i (to the upper-left circled corner). So the square is {sM + t·iM : 0 ≤ s,t ≤ 1}. A half-open version contains exactly N(M) = 377 Gaussian integers. This is what the next page calls 'den vollen Quadranten von M'.

(c) Halving. Two heavy freehand lines join the midpoints of opposite sides. They cut the quadrant into four squares with edges M/2 and iM/2. These lines are Re(z·conj(M)) = N(M)/2 and Im(z·conj(M)) = N(M)/2. Since N(M) is odd and Re(z·conj M) is an integer for z in Z[i], no lattice point lies on them (my inference). This is the Gaussian analogue of the half-system 1..(p-1)/2 in Gauss's lemma, and of Eisenstein's half-rectangle.

(d) Red 'Variegation'. In the sub-square at the corner iM, red lines join circled lattice points. Measured from iM, these points are iM+(5-2i), iM+2(5-2i) and iM+(5-2i)-i(5-2i). So the red net is the square grid of the lattice (5-2i)Z[i], with edges 5-2i and i(5-2i).

As read, 19+4i = (3+2i)(5-2i). So the red grid is the grid of spacing M/m with m = 3+2i, which is primary (3+2i ≡ 1 mod 2+2i). Equivalently it is the set of z where Re(z·m/M) or Im(z·m/M) is an integer. This matches the next page: 'mache dessen Durchschnitt mit m dessen Variegation'. Each Gaussian integer z then lies in a cell of this grid. Its 'Intersection' number is presumably formed with the bracket function [x] = (floor x + ceil x)/2 applied to the coordinates of z·m/M. The half-units at boundaries handle points that lie exactly on grid lines. That is what happens here, because in this example m divides M, so the grid nodes are lattice points.

(e) Pencil net. Faint pencil lines form a triangular/diagonal network over the whole quadrant. Their exact definition cannot be determined from the image; plausibly they are further grid or diagonal lines of the same construction.

(f) Small sketches. The lower-left sketch is a tilted cell on a few lattice points, cut into regions labelled 3, 2, 0, 1. These are evidently intersection counts of the pieces into which a lattice cell is cut by the grid. The lower-right sketch is a square cut by oblique lines into pieces labelled 1, 2, 1 / 2, 0, 1 / 1, 1, with hatched strips. It looks like the cut-and-shift bookkeeping of the next page: replace region Q''' by its image under -i, whose cells have intersection numbers one smaller, and so on.

No computations are written; the derivations themselves are on pp. 10–11.
errors: No arithmetic on the page, so nothing to falsify.

The lattice reading is approximate. If it is right, M = 19+4i is composite, 13·29 = (3+2i)(5-2i), and is divisible by the grid parameter. This is a degenerate or illustrative example, not a valid residue test (coprime M and m are needed). It was probably chosen so that the grid nodes fall on lattice points.
With 0 at the lower-left corner, 19+4i is not primary in Gauss's normalization (≡1 mod 2+2i); its associate -19-4i is. Orientation or associate choice is ambiguous.
The heavy dividing lines are freehand and slightly irregular; this is only a drawing imprecision.

results.what: Representation of the residue system mod M by the Gaussian integers in the square spanned by M and iM (the 'full quadrant'), with N(M) points, and its division into four half-squares avoiding lattice points because N(M) is odd.
results.modern_name: Fundamental domain of Z[i]/MZ[i]; Gaussian analogue of the half-system in Gauss's lemma
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum II, 1832); geometric use by Eisenstein (1844)

results.what: Overlaying the grid of spacing M/m (the 'Variegation' of m) on the quadrant and attaching to each lattice point an 'intersection' count via the half-counting bracket [x]. This is a lattice-point counting criterion for the biquadratic character (m/M)_4.
results.modern_name: Lattice-point (Eisenstein-type) proof or criterion for the quartic residue symbol; Gaussian-integer analogue of Gauss's lemma / Eisenstein's lattice proof
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein, 'Einfacher Beweis ... biquadratischen Reste' / lattice-point proofs (1844); for QR, Gauss's 3rd proof and Eisenstein's geometric version

deep.surprise_reason: It is known that Gauss had (unpublished) approaches to biquadratic reciprocity, and his Nachlass on biquadratic residues is partly printed in Werke II. A geometric lattice and grid counting criterion in Z[i], parallel to what Eisenstein published in 1844, is a notable detail but not a major unknown result. The page is only a figure, and its exact content depends on surrounding pages that may already be edited.

checkable.asserts: As read, M = 19+4i is the product of the primary m = 3+2i and the red-grid edge 5-2i.
N(M) = 377 = 13*29, the number of Gaussian integers in a half-open full quadrant of M.
Gives -6+11i, a Gaussian integer, so -19-4i is the primary associate of 19+4i.

checkable.sympy: len([(x,y) for x in range(-30,31) for y in range(-30,31) if 0<=Rational(x*19+y*4,377)<1 and 0<=Rational(-x*4+y*19,377)<1]) == 377
checkable.asserts: The half-open square spanned by M = 19+4i and iM contains exactly N(M) lattice points.
No lattice point lies on the midlines that cut the quadrant into four half-squares, since N(M) is odd.

checkable.asserts: The bracket function of p.10, [x] = (floor x + ceil x)/2, satisfies [x+k] = [x]+k and [-x] = -[x].

transcription_corrections: The lattice is a square lattice Z[i] with crosses and dots in checkerboard pattern (the two classes mod 1+i), not merely 'rectangular'.
Two corners of the large square are circled lattice points: lower left (= 0) and upper left (= iM).
The red lines in the upper-left sub-square form a square grid (edge about 5-2i in lattice units) through circled lattice points, not just triangles.
The two heavy lines dividing the large square run through the midpoints of its sides and extend slightly beyond it.
The lower-right sketch also contains hatched or ticked strips along its right edge and lower right.
